title: Four Doors Out: Dividend, Interest, Fee or Return of Capital
summary: Profit earned in one country reaches its owner in another through one of four doors: a dividend, interest on a loan, a fee for services, or a return of the capital invested. Each door has its own tax character, its own legal conditions and its own withholding. Choosing the door, and building it before the money arrives, is what repatriation planning means.
body:
Money does not simply come home; it leaves through one of four doors, dividend, interest, fee or return of capital, and each door is taxed, documented and policed differently, so you choose and build the door before the profit exists.

Recall

Q. How is a tax treaty read?

A. In good faith, by the ordinary meaning of its words in context and in light of its purpose, with the official commentary and domestic law alongside. It can only limit tax domestic law imposes.

Q. What is the difference between where a company is incorporated and where it is resident?

A. Incorporation is where it was legally formed. Residence for tax can follow where its real strategic decisions are made, so the two can differ.

Q. What is the critical path in a schedule?

A. The longest chain of dependent activities through the project. Any delay on it delays completion, because it has no float.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a cross-border project can be profitable, well financed and fully let, and still disappoint its owner, because the cash cannot get home cheaply or at all. The gap between profit earned in the project country and cash spendable by the owner is called leakage, and repatriation is the discipline of keeping it small and predictable. Every investor you bring in will ask how they get paid. Every lender will ask what leaves before it is repaid. Your answer is a choice among four doors, made at the start, not improvised when the first distribution is due.

The first door: dividends

In plain English: the project company pays its owner a share of its profit.

The professional framing: a dividend is paid out of after-tax profit, so the project country has already taxed the income. Corporate law usually allows it only if the company passes a solvency test, meaning it can pay its debts as they fall due after paying, or has enough distributable profits, depending on the jurisdiction [unverified — confirm independently]. The source country may then apply dividend withholding, possibly reduced by treaty. The home country may tax the dividend, credit the foreign tax, or exempt it, as last week showed.

Applied: a dividend is the honest default. Its weakness is that it can only follow accounting profit. A new building with heavy depreciation can generate plenty of cash while showing little profit, and cash with no distributable profit behind it may be stuck.

The second door: interest

In plain English: the owner lends the project money instead of, or as well as, investing equity, and the project pays interest.

The professional framing: interest is usually deductible to the payer, reducing project-country corporate tax, and usually taxed to the recipient. It often carries its own withholding, again possibly reduced by treaty. Deductibility is limited by rules on thin capitalisation and interest caps, which Omar and Nadia teach in Week 60, and the loan must be real: documented, at a commercial rate, with a repayment schedule that is actually followed.

A worked example, hypothetical, with rates chosen only for arithmetic. A project earns 1,000,000 dollars before interest. Corporate tax: 25 percent. Dividend withholding: 15 percent. Interest withholding: 10 percent. Route A, all equity: corporate tax 250,000 dollars, dividend of 750,000 dollars, withholding 112,500 dollars, owner receives 637,500 dollars. Route B, the owner lends and receives 400,000 dollars of deductible interest: taxable profit falls to 600,000 dollars, corporate tax 150,000 dollars, dividend 450,000 dollars with withholding of 67,500 dollars, interest of 400,000 dollars with withholding of 40,000 dollars. Owner receives 382,500 plus 360,000, which is 742,500 dollars. The same profit, 105,000 dollars more cash, because the interest door was taxed once at a low withholding instead of twice. That is why interest-cap rules exist, and why a lender's view of shareholder loans matters.

Say that out loud now.

Dividend from profit, interest from a real loan, fee for a real service, return of capital from capital actually put in.

The third door: fees

In plain English: the owner's company provides services to the project, such as development management, asset management or design coordination, and charges for them.

The professional framing: fees are usually deductible to the project and taxable to the recipient, sometimes subject to withholding and to indirect tax such as value-added tax. They must be for real services, actually performed, at an arm's-length price, which is the subject of transfer pricing in Week 61. A fee for nothing is not a fee; it is a disguised dividend, and an authority can recharacterise it, deny the deduction, and charge withholding at the dividend rate on top.

The fourth door: return of capital

In plain English: you take back what you put in, rather than what the project earned.

The professional framing: a return of capital reduces paid-up or stated capital, a corporate-law account recording what shareholders contributed. In many systems it can be paid free of dividend withholding and is not income to the recipient up to the capital contributed, though it reduces the recipient's tax cost of the shares [unverified — confirm independently]. It needs a formal corporate step, usually a resolution and sometimes a solvency statement or court or creditor process, and records that prove what was contributed and when.

A second worked example, hypothetical. An owner contributed 3,000,000 dollars of equity and the project refinances, releasing 2,000,000 dollars of cash with little profit behind it. As a dividend, it may be impossible, for lack of distributable profit, or fully taxable. As a return of capital, if the records show 3,000,000 dollars of paid-up capital, 2,000,000 dollars can come home as a reduction of capital, leaving 1,000,000 dollars of capital and a lower share cost for the eventual sale. Records turned a stuck refinancing into a clean distribution.

How the best do it

Experienced cross-border sponsors write a repatriation plan into the structure memo on day one: which doors each entity will use, in what order, under what conditions, with what withholding, and what records each door requires. They capitalise projects so that every door is open on purpose, a documented shareholder loan, a services agreement with a real scope, and accurate capital records, rather than discovering at the first distribution that only one door works. A small developer can copy that with a single page attached to the structure chart.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: each door has a different character, withholding and home treatment. Liability: directors who pay a dividend or reduce capital without passing the legal test can be personally exposed. Banking: lenders restrict every door through distribution covenants and subordination of shareholder loans. Governance: each payment needs the right resolution, signed by those with authority. Estate: a shareholder loan is an asset of the lender's estate and must be documented to be collected. Exit: returning capital early lowers share cost and so raises the taxable gain on sale.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in both countries, and corporate lawyer on solvency and capital-reduction steps.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is building the project with one door, usually dividends, and finding that cash is trapped behind missing profit, a covenant or a high withholding rate. The control is a repatriation plan in the structure memo, with every intended door documented before the first dollar of equity goes in.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sends money in as plain equity with no record of the amount and date, then cannot prove paid-up capital when he wants it back.

Callback

In Week 11, Nadia taught that cash and profit are different things. Repatriation is where that difference costs money: dividends follow profit, but you live on cash, and the other three doors exist largely to bridge the gap.

Recap

Four doors bring money home: dividend from distributable profit, interest from a documented loan, fee for a real service at arm's length, and return of capital from recorded contributions. Each carries its own tax, withholding and legal conditions. Choose and document them before the money exists.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Argentina in 2001 and 2002, when foreign investors' cash could not get home.
checklist: My structure memo names the doors each entity will use to pay money home.
I know the dividend test, solvency or distributable profit, in the project country.
Any shareholder loan is documented, at a commercial rate, with a schedule followed in practice.
Every fee is for a real, defined service, priced at arm's length.
I have records of every capital contribution, its amount and its date.
I know the withholding on each door, with and without a treaty.
I know how my lender's covenants restrict each door.
Directors know the legal test they must pass before any distribution.
head: Field checklist
speak: Profit earned abroad comes home through one of four doors. A dividend is paid from after-tax profit and needs the company to pass a solvency or distributable-profit test; then withholding may apply. Interest is paid on a real, documented loan; it is usually deductible to the project and carries its own, often lower, withholding, which is why interest-cap rules exist. A fee is paid for a real service at an arm's-length price; a fee for nothing is a disguised dividend. A return of capital gives back what was actually contributed; with good capital records it can often be paid without dividend withholding, though it lowers the cost of the shares. In my hypothetical example, mixing interest with dividends sent 105,000 dollars more cash home from the same profit. The lesson is to choose and document the doors on day one, because cash that has only one door often gets stuck.
terms: Repatriation — moving profit or capital from the country where it is earned or held back to the owner's home country.
Leakage — the difference between profit earned in the project and cash actually spendable by the owner after all taxes and costs on the way home.
Return of capital — a payment that reduces the shareholders' contributed capital rather than distributing profit.

hostile.q: Your shareholder loan cuts the project's tax. Why won't the authority treat the interest as a disguised dividend?
hostile.a: Because it is a real loan on commercial terms. It is documented, the rate is supported by a pricing analysis, the repayment schedule is followed, and the debt sits within the project country's interest limits and our lender's subordination agreement. I have modelled the case where part of the interest is disallowed, and the project still works. If any of those facts weakens, we pay more of the cash out as dividends.

title: Argentina 2001 and 2002: When Cash Could Not Come Home
summary: Argentina pegged its peso to the United States dollar through the 1990s, then in late 2001 and early 2002 froze bank withdrawals, defaulted on public debt, abandoned the peg and converted dollar contracts into pesos. Foreign investors with cash in the country found every door home closed or narrowed at once. This lesson takes the episode through seven steps from a repatriation angle, without inventing figures.
body:
In Argentina at the end of 2001 and the start of 2002, the rules for getting money out changed in weeks, and investors who had planned to repatriate later learned that a door you have not used is a door you may never get to use.

Recall

Q. What is the credit cap?

A. The limit, usually the home tax on a piece of foreign income, above which foreign tax cannot be credited. Foreign tax above it is wasted unless domestic law allows a carryover.

Q. Why can a substance problem not be cured backward?

A. Because substance is proved by records made at the time, showing who decided and where. Meetings held later cannot show that past decisions were made somewhere they were not.

Q. Who owns float in a schedule?

A. Unless the contract says otherwise, float is commonly treated as shared by the project, so the first party to need it uses it. Many owners write the answer into the contract because the default is disputed.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me today because this failure is told in currency, law and timing at once. Yesterday Devika taught four doors. This case shows what happens when a government closes or narrows them together, and why the safest repatriation plan moves money on a schedule rather than waiting for a perfect moment. Facts below are the broad, well-documented outline of the episode. I give no figures I cannot stand behind; where I describe size, I describe it in words.

1. Timeline

In 1991, Argentina adopted a convertibility law that fixed the peso at one to one with the United States dollar, backed by reserves, to end years of severe inflation. Through the 1990s, inflation fell and foreign investment flowed in, much of it into utilities, banks and property. Many contracts and bank deposits were written in dollars. In the late 1990s the economy entered a long recession, public debt rose and confidence fell. In December 2001 the government restricted cash withdrawals from banks, a measure that became known as the corralito. Within weeks there were riots, the president resigned, and the government announced it would suspend payments on much of its public debt. In January 2002 the peg was abandoned and the peso fell sharply. Dollar deposits and many dollar contracts were converted into pesos at rates set by government, and controls limited transfers of money abroad.

2. Key decisions

From an investor's chair, three decisions mattered. Keeping operating cash and accumulated profits in the country, often in local banks, on the assumption it could leave at will. Writing revenue contracts that depended on the peg holding, without a plan if it did not. And deferring repatriation, sometimes for tax or reinvestment reasons that made sense in isolation, until after the rules changed.

3. Assumptions

The central assumption was that convertibility was the law and would stay the law. A second was that bank deposits were cash. A third was that a foreign investor's rights to transfer profits abroad, often protected by bilateral investment treaties and local law, would be honoured in practice and in time. Many investors later pursued claims through international arbitration under investment treaties; those processes took years and outcomes varied [unverified — confirm independently]. A claim is not cash.

Say that out loud now.

A claim is not cash, and a door I have not used may close before I need it.

4. Incentives

Local managers were rewarded on local results, often in local terms, and had little reason to push cash out of the business. Group treasuries earned higher local interest rates by leaving cash in the country. Tax planning sometimes favoured holding profits offshore of the parent until a convenient time. Each incentive pointed toward leaving money where it was. None priced the chance of the doors closing together.

5. Warning signs ignored

The warning signs were public: years of recession, a rising public debt burden, falling reserves, widening spreads on government bonds, and deposits leaving the banking system in the months before the freeze. Each was visible to anyone who read the financial press. What made them easy to ignore was that the peg had held for a decade, and a long period of stability is a powerful anchor. Kema's Week 3 lesson on anchoring applies directly.

6. Point of no return

For an investor with cash in a local bank, the point of no return was the withdrawal freeze in December 2001. Before it, the choice to move money was still a commercial decision with a tax cost. After it, the choice belonged to the government. Every later step, the default, the devaluation, the conversion of dollar contracts, narrowed the options further.

7. Root cause

From a repatriation angle, the root cause was treating the ability to move money as permanent, and therefore deferring it. A peg is a policy, not a law of nature. A transfer right is a promise, not a wire.

The developer's version, hypothetical

Translate this to a project. A foreign-owned residential building earns 2,000,000 dollars a year of distributable cash. The owner leaves three years of it, 6,000,000 dollars, in a local account, intending to reinvest. A freeze and devaluation arrive. If the local currency loses, say, two thirds of its value against the home currency before any transfer is possible, the 6,000,000 dollars is worth 2,000,000 dollars at home, before any tax. An owner who swept cash home each quarter would have had at most one quarter's cash, 500,000 dollars, exposed.

A second worked example. The owner instead kept the cash at home but financed the building locally in home currency with rents in local currency. Devaluation does not trap cash here; it raises the debt service measured in local rent by three times, and the debt service coverage ratio collapses. Roman's point: repatriation risk and currency mismatch are cousins. Week 43 taught the second; this week is the first.

What a sweep policy looks like

Roman's version fits on half a page. Distributable cash, defined as cash above operating needs, debt service, required reserves and a stated local buffer, moves home within a set number of days after each quarter closes. The local buffer is sized in months of operating cost, not as a round number someone liked. Any exception, such as holding cash for a capital project, needs a written decision naming the amount, the reason, the date it will be reviewed and the person accountable. Treasury reports cash by country and currency every month. That is all. Its power is that it makes leaving money behind a decision someone has to sign, rather than the default nobody notices.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting distributable cash accumulate in the project country because it is convenient, earns interest or saves tax. The control is a written sweep policy: distributable cash moves home on a fixed schedule through pre-built doors, and any decision to leave it is recorded with its reason and reviewed each quarter.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes that if transfer abroad is legal today, it will be legal when he needs it. The second beginner's mistake is to price the tax on repatriating and never price the risk of not repatriating.

Callback

In Week 43, Roman taught convertibility and transfer risk and political-risk insurance as country-risk concepts. This case is those concepts arriving together, in weeks. Insurance and treaty protections may help after the event; only a sweep schedule helps before it.

Recap

A decade-long peg ended in a deposit freeze, a debt default, a devaluation and the conversion of dollar contracts, and money that had not already left the country was trapped or shrank. The prevention is to move distributable cash home on schedule, through doors built in advance.

Rule 58: Never let distributable cash accumulate behind a door you have not tested; build and use the repatriation route on a fixed schedule, and record every decision to leave money in the project country.

Next: Nadia on The Money: measuring leakage and the cost of trapped cash.
checklist: I have a written cash sweep policy for every project-country entity.
Each door home has been used at least once, so I know it works.
I record every decision to leave distributable cash in the project country, with its reason.
I know where project cash is held, in which banks and currencies.
I watch reserves, bond spreads and deposit flows in each country where I hold cash.
I have considered political-risk insurance and investment-treaty protection, with an adviser.
I have modelled a freeze and a devaluation against cash held locally.
head: Field checklist
speak: In 1991 Argentina fixed its peso at one to one with the dollar. It held for a decade, and foreign investment poured in, with many deposits and contracts written in dollars. Then a long recession and rising debt eroded confidence. In December 2001 the government froze bank withdrawals, the corralito. Within weeks it suspended payments on much of its debt, and in January 2002 it abandoned the peg. The peso fell sharply, dollar deposits and contracts were converted into pesos, and transfers abroad were restricted. Investors who had left profits in the country, to earn interest or reinvest later, found the doors home closed or narrowed together. Claims under investment treaties took years. The root cause, from a repatriation angle, was treating the ability to move money as permanent. Rule 58: never let distributable cash accumulate behind a door you have not tested; move it home on a fixed schedule.
terms: Currency board or peg — a policy fixing a currency's value to another, typically backed by reserves, which a government can abandon.
Capital controls — government restrictions on moving money into or out of a country, including limits on withdrawals and transfers abroad.
Cash sweep — a standing instruction moving surplus cash from an operating account to another account or entity on a fixed schedule.

hostile.q: Why should we let you send cash home every quarter instead of keeping it in the project for reinvestment?
hostile.a: Because cash in the project country carries a risk that cash at home does not: it can be frozen, devalued or blocked from transfer, and the warning can be very short. Sweeping on schedule limits the exposure to one quarter's cash. If a reinvestment needs the money, we send it back in through a documented door, with a record of why. I would rather pay the cost of moving it twice than learn in a crisis that the door was shut.

rule: Rule 58: Never let distributable cash accumulate behind a door you have not tested; build and use the repatriation route on a fixed schedule, and record every decision to leave money in the project country.

title: Measuring Leakage and the Cost of Trapped Cash
summary: Leakage is every dollar lost between profit earned in the project and cash in the owner's hands: corporate tax, withholding, home tax, conversion spread, bank and compliance costs, and the delay itself. Measure it as a percentage of pre-tax profit, then add the cost of cash that cannot move. Small differences compound into large ones over a hold period.
body:
Leakage is a single number you can measure: the share of each pre-tax dollar the project earns that never reaches you, and once you measure it every year, you can manage it.

Recall

Q. In tax diligence, what is the question behind every question?

A. How much could this cost the buyer, and how likely is it? Help them size it honestly, then offer a mechanism, such as a capped indemnity or an escrow, to allocate it.

Q. What is the value of a substance record to an investor?

A. It is the evidence that a structure's tax position rests on facts, which lowers the risk the investor must price and so raises what the structure is worth.

Q. What is a baseline schedule review?

A. The owner's check of the contractor's first full schedule for logic, durations, float and completeness before it is accepted as the measure of progress and delay.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two structures can earn the same profit and deliver very different cash. Over a ten-year hold, a few percentage points of leakage a year is the difference between a good investment and an average one. And leakage is not only tax. Currency conversion, banking fees, audit and compliance costs, and the time money spends waiting all take their slice. Nadia's job is to make that slice visible.

The leakage stack

In plain English: start with a dollar of pre-tax profit in the project and count everything that disappears before it is spendable at home.

The professional framing: build a leakage stack with six layers. One, project-country corporate tax. Two, withholding on the door used. Three, home-country tax after credits or exemption. Four, conversion cost: the spread between the market exchange rate and the rate your bank gives, plus wire fees. Five, compliance cost: audits, tax filings in both countries, transfer-pricing files and substance costs, allocated to the cash moved. Six, the time cost: interest or return foregone while money sits waiting to be moved. Leakage percentage is the sum of the six divided by pre-tax profit.

A worked example, hypothetical, with rates chosen only for arithmetic. A project earns 2,000,000 dollars before tax. Layer one, corporate tax at 25 percent: 500,000 dollars. Layer two, dividend withholding at 10 percent on the 1,500,000 dollar dividend: 150,000 dollars. Layer three, the home country exempts the dividend: zero. Layer four, a conversion spread of 1 percent on the 1,350,000 dollars converted: 13,500 dollars. Layer five, compliance costs of 60,000 dollars a year. Layer six, cash moved only once a year, on average six months after it was earned, at a 6 percent opportunity cost on about 1,350,000 dollars: roughly 40,500 dollars. Total leakage: 764,000 dollars, or 38.2 percent of pre-tax profit. The owner receives about 1,236,000 dollars of usable value.

Say that out loud now.

Leakage is every slice between project profit and spendable cash at home, divided by the profit.

Which layers you can move

Layer one is mostly set by the project country's law and the building's tax depreciation. Layers two and three are set by the door, the treaty and the home relief method, Devika's and Elias's subjects. Layer four is a banking negotiation: on large, regular conversions, a better rate or a forward contract can matter. Layer five is a question of whether each entity earns its cost. Layer six is a choice of sweep frequency, and it connects directly to yesterday's case.

Continue the example. Change the door mix so that 400,000 dollars is paid as documented shareholder interest with 5 percent withholding, which is deductible. Corporate tax falls to 400,000 dollars on 1,600,000 dollars of profit. The dividend is 1,200,000 dollars, withholding 120,000 dollars. Interest withholding 20,000 dollars. Home tax on interest, at a hypothetical 30 percent with a credit for the 20,000 dollars: 100,000 dollars. Sweep quarterly, so the average wait is about six weeks and the time cost falls to roughly 10,000 dollars. Conversion and compliance roughly unchanged at about 75,000 dollars. Total leakage about 725,000 dollars, 36.3 percent. A modest change, and notice where it came from: the interest door saved corporate tax but was taxed at home, so most of the gain came from sweeping more often.

Leakage over a hold period

Annual leakage compounds into the equity result. Suppose two structures each earn 2,000,000 dollars a year before tax for ten years. One leaks 38 percent, the other 33 percent. The difference is 5 percent of 2,000,000 dollars, 100,000 dollars a year. At a 10 percent discount rate, ten years of 100,000 dollars has a present value of about 614,000 dollars. On a project with, say, 12,000,000 dollars of equity, that is about 5 percent of the equity invested, earned or lost by structure and process alone, with no change to the building. That is why Nadia insists the stack is computed every year, not once at the start: rates change, treaties change, and a stack that was 33 percent in year 1 can drift.

Trapped cash has a price

Trapped cash is cash a project holds that cannot be paid out: blocked by a covenant, missing distributable profit, a capital control, or a door not yet built. It is still on the balance sheet, so it looks like value. It is worth less than its face, because you cannot use it, and it is exposed to the project country's currency and banking system.

A second worked example. A project holds 3,000,000 dollars it cannot distribute for two years because the lender's distribution test is failing. At a 10 percent required return, its value today to the owner is about 3,000,000 divided by 1.21, about 2,479,000 dollars, before any currency risk. If you assign, say, a 15 percent chance that the local currency falls by half before the cash can move, the expected loss is 15 percent of 1,500,000 dollars, 225,000 dollars, so a fair value nearer 2,250,000 dollars. A quarter of the cash has gone without a single transaction.

Notice that trapped cash also distorts the leakage stack. Cash that cannot move has not leaked yet, so a stack computed only on cash actually distributed can look excellent in a year when nothing moved at all. Report the stack and the trapped-cash line together, so a good leakage number in a bad year cannot hide the bad year.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note: on your personal balance sheet, value cross-border holdings at the after-leakage cash they can deliver, not at the profit they report, and mark trapped cash below its face. A balance sheet that counts trapped cash at par overstates your liquidity floor, the minimum of truly available cash you set for yourself in Week 7. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is measuring a cross-border project by reported profit, so leakage and trapped cash stay invisible until a distribution disappoints. The control is a leakage stack computed every year for every entity, and a trapped-cash line in every report.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts only tax and forgets conversion spread, compliance cost and the time money waits. On a modest project the non-tax layers can be a large share of the total.

Professional sign-off required: chartered accountant on the stack, and tax adviser in each country on the tax layers.

Callback

In Week 12, Nadia taught that owner reporting should show what the owner actually needs to decide. A leakage stack is that idea across a border: it turns a tax problem into one line an owner can read, compare year to year and act on.

Recap

Leakage is the share of pre-tax profit that never reaches you, in six layers: corporate tax, withholding, home tax, conversion, compliance and time. Measure it yearly. Value trapped cash below its face, discounted for delay and currency risk. Sweep frequency is often the cheapest lever.

Next: Elias on The Rules: withholding mechanics, dividend and capital-reduction tests, and who is liable when withholding goes wrong.
checklist: I compute a six-layer leakage stack each year for every cross-border entity.
I state leakage as a percentage of pre-tax profit.
I know my conversion spread and have asked my bank to improve it.
I allocate compliance and substance costs to the cash they help move.
I have chosen a sweep frequency and priced the time cost of waiting.
Every report shows trapped cash on its own line.
I value trapped cash below face for delay and currency risk.
head: Field checklist
speak: Leakage is every slice lost between profit earned in the project and cash I can spend at home. I measure it in six layers: project-country corporate tax, withholding on the door used, home-country tax after credit or exemption, the currency conversion spread and wire fees, compliance costs such as audits and filings in both countries, and the time cost of money waiting to move. I add the six and divide by pre-tax profit. In my hypothetical example that came to about 38 percent. Some layers are set by law, but the door mix, the bank's conversion rate and the sweep frequency are mine to change, and sweeping more often was the cheapest lever. Trapped cash, blocked by a covenant, missing profit or capital controls, is worth less than its face: discount it for delay and for currency risk. I put leakage and trapped cash on their own lines in every report.
terms: Leakage stack — a layer-by-layer count of every tax, cost and delay between project profit and spendable cash at home.
Conversion spread — the difference between the market exchange rate and the rate a bank actually applies to a currency conversion.
Trapped cash — cash held by an entity that cannot currently be distributed, for legal, contractual or regulatory reasons.

hostile.q: Your report shows 3,000,000 dollars of cash in the project company. How much of it can you actually pay us?
hostile.a: None of it this quarter. The lender's distribution test is not met, so it is trapped until it is. I show it on its own line for that reason, and I value it below face in my own numbers because of the delay and the currency exposure. We expect the test to clear in two quarters on the current lease-up; if it does not, I will tell you before the next report.

title: Withholding, Distribution Tests and Who Pays When It Goes Wrong
summary: Withholding is an obligation of the payer, not the recipient, which is why your own project company is usually liable if the wrong rate is applied. Dividends and capital reductions must also pass corporate-law tests, and lenders add their own. This lesson teaches the concepts; every rate, form and deadline must be verified against the primary source.
body:
When a cross-border payment goes wrong, the tax authority usually collects from the payer, your own project company, so withholding is your obligation even when the tax is someone else's.

Recall

Q. Can a tax treaty create a tax?

A. No. It can only reduce or remove tax that domestic law imposes.

Q. Why do contemporaneous records matter for residence?

A. Because residence often turns on where decisions were really made, and only records made at the time can prove it convincingly.

Q. What is a three-week look-ahead schedule?

A. A short-range, detailed schedule of the next few weeks' work, built from the master schedule by the people doing the work, used to plan crews, materials and constraints.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, repatriation is not only a tax calculation; it is a sequence of legal acts, each with its own conditions. A dividend declared without passing the corporate test can be recovered from shareholders and can expose directors. A payment withheld at the wrong rate leaves the payer owing the difference. A distribution made in breach of a loan covenant is an event of default. Get the sequence right and money moves cleanly. Get one step wrong and a routine payment becomes a liability with your name on it. This lesson teaches concepts; verify every rate, form, deadline and section against the primary source before you rely on it.

How withholding works

In plain English: the country where the payer sits makes the payer collect the tax from the payment and send it in, because it cannot easily chase a foreign recipient.

The professional framing: domestic law imposes a tax on certain payments to non-residents, such as dividends, interest, rents, royalties and some service fees, and appoints the payer as collection agent. The payer must withhold at the correct rate, remit to the authority by a deadline, and usually file a return showing payments and recipients. If a treaty reduces the rate, the payer may apply it at source if it holds the evidence the law requires, often a residence certificate and a declaration of beneficial ownership, or the payer withholds the full rate and the recipient claims a refund later [unverified — confirm independently]. If the payer applies a reduced rate without proper support and the claim fails, the payer is commonly liable for the shortfall, plus interest and possibly penalties.

A worked example, hypothetical. A project company pays a 1,000,000 dollar dividend to a foreign parent and applies a 5 percent treaty rate instead of a domestic 20 percent, withholding 50,000 dollars and sending 950,000 dollars. On audit, the treaty claim fails. The authority assesses the project company for 150,000 dollars, plus interest. The money has already left. The project company must pay it from its own cash and then try to recover it from the parent, which may be unwilling or, if things have gone badly, unable.

Say that out loud now.

The payer withholds, the payer remits, and the payer pays if the rate was wrong.

The corporate-law tests

Before tax even arises, corporate law decides whether money may leave the company at all. For a dividend, many systems apply a solvency test: after paying, can the company pay its debts as they fall due, and do its assets exceed its liabilities? Others require distributable profits, a defined accounting figure [unverified — confirm independently]. A capital reduction often needs a special resolution, a solvency statement or a creditor or court process. Directors who approve a distribution that fails the test can be personally liable, and shareholders who knew may have to give it back.

Applied: before every distribution, require a short distribution memo from your finance lead: the test that applies, the figures that pass it, the board resolution, the withholding rate and its support, and the covenant check. Sign nothing without it.

The lender's tests

Your loan agreement adds its own gates. Typical distribution conditions, which are commercial practice and not law, include no event of default, a minimum debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) measured over a past period and sometimes projected, required reserves fully funded, and delivery of financial statements. Shareholder loans are usually subordinated: payments of interest or principal to the owner are allowed only when the distribution test is met, or not at all until the senior loan is repaid. A cash management agreement may route all revenue through a lender-controlled account with a waterfall: operating costs, debt service, reserves, and only then the owner.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A project's loan requires a trailing DSCR of 1.25 before any distribution. Net operating income (NOI) over the last twelve months is 2,400,000 dollars and debt service is 2,000,000 dollars, a DSCR of 1.20. Distributable cash of 400,000 dollars exists, the tax and corporate tests would allow a dividend, and the dividend is still forbidden. Paying it anyway, or disguising it as a fee to the owner's company, is a default. The cash is trapped until NOI rises to 2,500,000 dollars or debt service falls.

The order of the gates

Run the three gates in a fixed order, because each later one assumes the earlier ones passed. First the loan: if the distribution test fails, nothing else matters this quarter, and you save the cost of the rest. Second corporate law: compute distributable profit or run the solvency test on current figures, and have the board resolve. Third withholding: confirm the door, the rate and the evidence, then pay and remit by the deadline and file the return. A useful habit is a one-page distribution calendar for each entity, showing the quarter-end, the covenant test date, the board meeting, the payment date and the withholding remittance date, so the gates are passed in sequence rather than by memory.

Indirect tax on the fee door

A fee from the project to the owner's company can also attract value-added tax or goods and services tax, depending on where the service is treated as supplied and whether reverse-charge rules apply, and the fee may face its own withholding [unverified — confirm independently]. Indirect tax is often recoverable by a registered business, but only with correct invoices and registration. A fee door built without asking the indirect tax question can cost a non-recoverable slice on every payment.

A practical point on refunds. Where the payer withholds the full domestic rate and the recipient must claim a treaty refund, the money can be gone for a year or more and the claim needs the same evidence it would have needed at source. Build the refund timing into the leakage stack as a time cost, and ask whether applying the rate at source, with the evidence filed, is the better route.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a project company that applies a reduced treaty rate on the parent's say-so, without the evidence the law requires, and becomes liable for the shortfall after the cash has gone. The control is a withholding file for each recipient, refreshed at least yearly, and a rule that no reduced rate is applied without it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks tax and forgets the corporate test and the loan covenants, or checks the covenants and forgets the withholding return. All three gates must open, in that order.

Professional sign-off required: corporate lawyer on the distribution test, tax adviser on withholding, and borrower's counsel on the covenants.

Callback

In Week 39, Priya taught covenants and events of default in a construction loan. Distribution covenants are the same machinery after completion. They decide whether the four doors Devika taught on Day 1 are open in any given quarter, whatever tax and corporate law allow.

Recap

Withholding is the payer's obligation: withhold, remit, file, and pay if the rate was wrong. Corporate law decides whether money may leave, through solvency or distributable-profit tests. The loan decides whether it may leave now. A distribution memo checks all three before any payment.

Next: Devika on The Numbers: reverse engineering a target net distribution back to the gross payment needed through each door.
checklist: I keep a withholding file for each foreign recipient, refreshed yearly.
No reduced treaty rate is applied without the evidence the law requires.
I know the withholding remittance and filing obligations in the project country.
I know whether dividends are tested on solvency or distributable profits.
Each distribution is supported by a written distribution memo and a board resolution.
I know my loan's distribution conditions and subordination terms.
I have checked indirect tax on every fee door.
I never disguise a blocked distribution as a fee or a loan repayment.
head: Field checklist
speak: Repatriation is a sequence of legal gates. First, corporate law: a dividend must pass a solvency or distributable-profit test, and a capital reduction needs its own resolution and sometimes a solvency statement; directors who approve a failing distribution can be personally exposed. Second, the loan: distribution conditions such as no default, a minimum DSCR and funded reserves can block cash that tax and corporate law would allow. Third, withholding: the payer, my own project company, must withhold at the right rate, remit and file. If it applies a treaty rate without the required evidence and the claim fails, the payer usually owes the shortfall, with interest, after the money has gone. Fee doors can also attract indirect tax. So before any payment I want a distribution memo covering the corporate test, the covenant check and the withholding rate with its support. All three gates must open.
terms: Collection agent — a person, usually the payer, whom tax law requires to withhold and remit tax on another's behalf.
Solvency test — a corporate-law condition that a company must remain able to pay its debts after a distribution.
Cash management agreement — a loan document routing project revenue through controlled accounts in a fixed order of payment.

hostile.q: You applied the treaty rate on last year's dividends. If it is wrong, who pays, and from what?
hostile.a: The project company pays, as the payer, so I treat it as our risk, not the parent's. That is why we hold the residence certificate and the beneficial-ownership declaration the law requires before we apply the rate, refreshed each year, and why the parent has signed an indemnity in the project company's favour. I can show you the withholding file for each payment.

title: Reverse Engineering a Target Distribution Through Each Door
summary: Start from the cash the owner wants to receive at home and work backward to the project profit and gross payment each door requires. The reverse calculation shows which door is cheapest for a given target, and how much more the project must earn to deliver it. All rates are hypothetical.
body:
If you know the cash you need at home, you can work backward through every tax layer to the profit the project must earn, and the door that needs the least profit is the cheapest way home.

Recall

Q. What are the four doors through which money comes home?

A. A dividend from distributable profit, interest on a documented loan, a fee for a real service at arm's length, and a return of recorded capital.

Q. Who owns a company's substance record?

A. The company itself, through its directors and secretary. It must be kept by those who make the decisions, where they make them, not assembled by a parent later.

Q. What is the Last Planner System?

A. A collaborative planning method in which the people who do the work commit to weekly tasks they can actually complete, with constraints removed in advance, and track the percentage of promises kept.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, investors and lenders talk in targets. "We need 1,000,000 dollars a year in hand." Working forward from profit, you can only report what arrives. Working backward from the target, you discover what the project must earn and which door delivers it most cheaply. This is the even-week drill: start from the finished outcome and reverse engineer it. Every rate below is hypothetical, chosen only so the arithmetic is visible; verify real rates against the primary source before you rely on them.

The setup

Target: 1,000,000 dollars of cash in the owner's hands at home, after all tax, each year. Project-country corporate tax: 25 percent. Dividend withholding: 10 percent. Interest withholding: 10 percent. Fee withholding: 15 percent. Home tax on dividends: exempt. Home tax on interest and fees: 30 percent, with a credit for withholding. Interest and fees are deductible to the project, within limits we assume are met.

Door 1: dividend, worked backward

Step 1. Home tax is nil, so the owner needs 1,000,000 dollars after withholding.

Step 2. Withholding is 10 percent of the gross dividend, so the owner keeps 90 percent. Gross dividend equals 1,000,000 divided by 0.90, which is about 1,111,111 dollars.

Step 3. The dividend comes from after-tax profit, which is 75 percent of pre-tax profit. Pre-tax profit equals 1,111,111 divided by 0.75, which is about 1,481,481 dollars.

So to deliver 1,000,000 dollars by dividend, the project must earn about 1,481,000 dollars before tax. Leakage: about 481,000 dollars, or 32.5 percent of pre-tax profit.

Say that out loud now.

Divide by what is kept at each layer, working from home back to the project.

Door 2: interest, worked backward

Step 1. Home tax is 30 percent of the gross interest, with a credit for the 10 percent withheld, so net home tax is 20 percent of gross. Total tax on interest is 10 percent plus 20 percent, 30 percent of gross. The owner keeps 70 percent.

Step 2. Gross interest equals 1,000,000 divided by 0.70, about 1,428,571 dollars.

Step 3. Interest is deductible, so the project pays no corporate tax on profit used to pay it. Pre-tax profit needed: about 1,428,571 dollars.

The interest door needs about 53,000 dollars less profit than the dividend door, under these assumptions, because it is taxed once at the higher home rate rather than twice. Leakage: 30 percent.

Door 3: fee, worked backward

Step 1. Withholding 15 percent, home tax 30 percent with a 15 percent credit: total 30 percent of gross. Owner keeps 70 percent.

Step 2. Gross fee: 1,000,000 divided by 0.70, about 1,428,571 dollars, the same as interest, before indirect tax.

Step 3. Now add indirect tax. If the fee attracts a hypothetical 15 percent value-added tax that the project cannot recover, because its residential rents are exempt supplies, the project's real cost is 1,428,571 times 1.15, about 1,642,857 dollars. The fee door is now the most expensive of the three. Devika's point: indirect tax on a fee is invisible in an income-tax model and decisive in a cash one.

Door 4: return of capital

If the owner has recorded paid-up capital and the corporate test is met, a return of capital may need only the cash itself, with no withholding and no home tax up to the cost of the shares, under these assumptions [unverified — confirm independently]. To deliver 1,000,000 dollars, the project needs 1,000,000 dollars of cash, whether or not it has profit. The catch: it is finite. Every dollar returned lowers the share cost, so the gain, and the tax, on eventual sale is higher by the same amount. Return of capital defers leakage; it rarely removes it.

DoorProject needs before taxLeakage share
Dividend1,481,48132.5 percent
Interest1,428,57130.0 percent
Fee, with unrecoverable indirect tax1,642,85739.1 percent
Return of capital1,000,000 of cashdeferred to sale

A second worked example: mixing doors

Doors are not either-or. Suppose interest is capped by thin-capitalisation rules at 600,000 dollars a year. Interest of 600,000 dollars delivers 420,000 dollars net. The remaining 580,000 dollars must come by dividend: gross dividend 580,000 divided by 0.90, about 644,444 dollars, needing pre-tax profit of 644,444 divided by 0.75, about 859,259 dollars. Total pre-tax profit needed: 600,000 plus 859,259, about 1,459,259 dollars. The mix sits between the pure doors, and the cap decides where.

Check by running forward

Take the dividend row and run it forward to prove it. Pre-tax profit 1,481,481 dollars. Corporate tax at 25 percent: 370,370 dollars. Dividend: 1,111,111 dollars. Withholding at 10 percent: 111,111 dollars. Home tax: nil. Cash in hand: 1,000,000 dollars. The row is right. Run the interest row: gross interest 1,428,571 dollars, withholding 142,857 dollars, home tax at 30 percent 428,571 dollars less a 142,857 dollar credit, 285,714 dollars. Cash in hand: 1,428,571 less 142,857 less 285,714, which is 1,000,000 dollars. Right again.

This check takes two minutes and catches almost every gross-up error. Make it a rule that no distribution target goes into an investor document until its row has been run both ways and the two directions agree to the dollar.

What the table does not show

The table compares doors under one year's tax. It does not show timing, such as when withholding is due against when a home credit is received, or the cost of building each door, such as loan documentation, a services agreement and its pricing study, or capital-reduction procedures. Add those as separate lines before choosing. A door that saves 50,000 dollars a year but costs 40,000 dollars a year to maintain is a door you probably do not need.

Last, remember that every rate in this table can change by budget, protocol or court decision. The method lasts; the numbers do not. Rebuild the table whenever a rate moves.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing a door on income tax alone and missing indirect tax, interest caps or covenants that change its cost. The control is to reverse engineer every target through all four doors, with indirect tax and limits included, before committing to a distribution policy.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner multiplies instead of divides: he takes 10 percent of 1,000,000 dollars, adds it back, and gets 1,100,000 dollars instead of 1,111,111. Gross-ups divide by what is kept.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in both countries, and an indirect tax specialist on any fee door.

Callback

Four lessons back, Elias worked one income stream forward through credit and exemption. Today's table is the same arithmetic run in reverse, and the two must agree: run any row forward and you should land on 1,000,000 dollars. If you do not, one of them is wrong.

Recap

Start from the cash target and divide by what is kept at each layer, home tax, then withholding, then corporate tax. Interest and fees avoid corporate tax but face home tax; fees may carry unrecoverable indirect tax; return of capital defers leakage to the sale. Caps and covenants decide the real mix.

Next: Roman on The Room: the lender meeting about distributions and shareholder loans.
checklist: I state every distribution target as cash in hand at home, after tax.
I reverse engineer each target through all four doors.
I divide by the share kept at each layer, never multiply and add back.
I include indirect tax on any fee door.
I apply interest caps and thin-capitalisation limits to the interest door.
I track paid-up capital and the share cost reduction from any return of capital.
I run each row forward to confirm it lands on the target.
head: Field checklist
speak: When an investor says they need 1,000,000 dollars a year in hand, I work backward. At each layer I divide by the share kept. For a dividend with home exemption, I divide 1,000,000 by 0.90 for withholding, then by 0.75 for corporate tax, and find the project must earn about 1.48 million before tax. For interest, which is deductible but taxed at home, I divide by 0.70 and need about 1.43 million. A fee looks the same until indirect tax is added; if the project cannot recover it, the fee becomes the most expensive door. A return of capital needs only the cash, but it lowers share cost, so it defers the tax to the sale rather than removing it. Real limits, like interest caps, push the answer toward a mix. And I check every row by running it forward to the target.
terms: Gross-up — calculating the larger payment needed so that a target amount remains after a deduction, by dividing by the share kept.
Exempt supply — a sale on which no value-added tax is charged and on which related input tax usually cannot be recovered.
Thin capitalisation — rules limiting interest deductions where a company is funded with too much debt relative to equity.

hostile.q: You say the interest door is cheapest. What stops the authority capping your interest deduction?
hostile.a: Nothing, if we exceed the limits, so I have modelled the cap. Under the project country's rules as our adviser reads them, interest above a certain level is not deductible, so I have limited shareholder interest to that level and sent the rest as dividends. The mix needs slightly more profit than pure interest would, and that mixed figure is the one in the investor model.

title: The Lender Meeting About Distributions and Shareholder Loans
summary: A senior lender will decide which repatriation doors are open each quarter. The scene shows how to negotiate distribution conditions and the treatment of a shareholder loan: what to ask for, what to concede, what never to say, the question behind the lender's questions, and how to hold your state. It closes with a thread on working with advisers.
body:
The senior lender controls which doors home are open each quarter, so negotiate the distribution test and the shareholder loan terms before the loan closes, when you still have leverage, not after, when you need the cash.

Recall

Q. In the Argentina case, what was the root cause from a repatriation angle?

A. Treating the ability to move money as permanent, and so deferring repatriation until the rules changed.

Q. What is the difference between residence and substance?

A. Residence is the legal conclusion about where an entity is taxable as a resident. Substance is the set of facts, people, decisions, premises and money, that supports that conclusion.

Q. What does percent plan complete measure in the Last Planner System?

A. The share of weekly commitments the team actually completed, a measure of planning reliability rather than progress.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, everything we built this week, the doors, the leakage stack, the reverse calculation, runs through the lender's loan agreement. A tight distribution test can trap cash for years in a building that is doing fine. A shareholder loan that the lender treats as equity can stop interest flowing home for the life of the loan. These terms are negotiated, not given. They are commercial practice, not law, and they are won or lost in one or two meetings.

The scene

A lender's office before a term sheet becomes a commitment. Across the table: the lender's credit officer and the relationship manager. The project, hypothetically, is a stabilising apartment building with forecast net operating income of 2,500,000 dollars and annual debt service of 1,800,000 dollars, a debt service coverage ratio of about 1.39. The draft term sheet allows distributions only above a trailing DSCR of 1.40, and treats your 4,000,000 dollar shareholder loan as fully subordinated, with no interest payable until the senior loan is repaid.

The credit officer opens: "We need the shareholder loan to sit behind us completely. Why should we let any money go to you before we're repaid?"

The lines to say

Bottom line first: "I accept that our loan sits behind yours in priority and on enforcement. I'm asking for current interest on it only when your distribution test is met, which is no more cash than you'd let us take as a dividend." That reframes the request: you are not asking for more cash out, only for the door it uses.

Then the test: "At 1.40 trailing, we fail by a hair in the first year and trap cash in a building that covers its debt comfortably. Could we set it at 1.30 for distributions, with a cash sweep to you above 1.40 if NOI falls, and a lock-up below 1.20?" A two-step test with a sweep gives the lender protection it values and you a door that opens.

Say that out loud now.

Our loan sits behind yours; I'm asking for the door, not for more cash.

The lines never to say

Never say "we'll just pay it as a management fee." It tells the lender you would route around its covenants, and it will tighten every clause in reply. Never say "the tax structure needs this." The lender does not care about your tax; it cares about its repayment. Never promise NOI you have not underwritten to win a looser test; if it fails, you have bought a covenant breach.

The question behind the question

When the credit officer asks why money should go to you first, he is really asking: if this building gets into trouble, how much cash will have walked out the door before I notice? Answer that question directly. Offer reporting, a lock-up trigger, and a cure right that requires you to put cash back in before any distribution resumes.

A worked example, hypothetical. Under the draft test, at DSCR 1.39, no distribution in year 1: 700,000 dollars of surplus cash trapped. Under your proposal, with distributions above 1.30, the 700,000 dollars can move, and interest on the shareholder loan at a hypothetical 8 percent, 320,000 dollars, travels by the interest door with lower leakage than a dividend. If NOI falls to 2,200,000 dollars, DSCR is about 1.22: distributions stop, and the lender's protection is unchanged from the draft.

A second worked example. The lender agrees, but asks for a reserve of six months' debt service, 900,000 dollars, funded before any distribution. That traps 900,000 dollars once, not every year. Accept it; it is the price of an open door. Ask that it be released when DSCR exceeds 1.50 for four quarters.

When to stay silent

After you propose the two-step test, stop. Let the credit officer work the numbers. If he says he must take it to committee, say "Thank you, what would committee want to see?" and then listen. Do not negotiate against yourself by offering a second concession before the first is answered.

Holding your state

Credit officers say no by default; it is their job. Hear "no" as "not yet, show me." Keep your voice slow and your numbers on paper, not in the air. If you feel pressure, return to the one sentence you came with.

And if committee says no to the whole proposal, have a fallback ready that costs the lender nothing: distributions above 1.40 as drafted, but tested on a forward twelve months of signed leases rather than trailing results, so a building in lease-up is judged on where it is going. Lenders will often accept a forward test with a haircut on unsigned space, and it can open the door two or three quarters earlier.

Working with advisers

This meeting is where three advisers' work must agree: your tax adviser's door design, your lawyer's drafting of the subordination and distribution clauses, and your accountant's covenant model. Before you walk in, put all three in one call and have each confirm, in writing, that the others' assumptions match theirs. Most repatriation failures are not one adviser's mistake but two advisers working from different versions.

And keep the decision in your hands. An adviser recommends; you decide, and you record why. Ask each adviser the same question at the end: "What would make you change this advice?" Their answer tells you what to monitor after the loan closes.

After the meeting

Within a day, send a short note to the relationship manager: what was proposed, what the credit officer asked to see, and when you will send it. It fixes your proposal in writing before committee meets, and it shows the discipline the lender will rely on for the life of the loan. Then put the open points in your decision journal, with the alternative you will accept if committee declines, so you are not deciding under pressure when the answer arrives.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting the lender's first distribution and subordination terms at term-sheet stage and discovering, a year after stabilisation, that every door is shut. The control is to model cash home under the draft terms before negotiating, and to bring a specific, priced alternative to the table.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the interest rate hard and the distribution test not at all. Over a long hold, the test can cost more than a quarter-point of rate.

Professional sign-off required: borrower's counsel on the loan and subordination agreements, and tax adviser on the shareholder loan.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught acknowledge, bridge, answer, and the line "I'll confirm by Friday." The credit officer's hardest question deserves exactly that: acknowledge his priority, bridge to the door, answer with a test and a trigger, and confirm anything you cannot price in the room.

Recap

The lender decides which doors are open. Accept priority, ask for the door, propose a two-step distribution test with a sweep and a lock-up, price every alternative, and never threaten to route around a covenant. Align your advisers before you walk in.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on repatriation, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill.
checklist: I have modelled cash home under the lender's draft distribution terms.
I bring a specific, priced alternative distribution test to the meeting.
I accept the lender's priority and ask only for the door.
I have proposed a reserve release trigger in exchange for any distribution reserve.
I never suggest routing a blocked distribution through fees.
My tax adviser, lawyer and accountant have confirmed matching assumptions in writing.
I have recorded why I chose each term and what would change my view.
head: Field checklist
speak: The senior lender controls which doors home are open each quarter, through the distribution test and the terms of any shareholder loan. I negotiate those terms before the commitment, while I have leverage. When the credit officer asks why any money should come to me before he is repaid, I answer the question behind it: how much cash could walk out before he notices. I accept that my loan sits behind his in priority, and ask only that it use the interest door when his distribution test is met, which is no more cash than he would allow as a dividend. Then I propose a two-step test, distributions above one level, a sweep to him below a higher one, a lock-up below a lower one, and accept a reserve with a release trigger. I never suggest routing cash through fees. And before I walk in, my tax adviser, lawyer and accountant confirm in writing that their assumptions match.
terms: Distribution test — a loan condition, often a minimum DSCR, that must be met before cash may be paid to the owner.
Lock-up — a loan provision that traps surplus cash in the project when a performance test falls below a set level.
Subordination — an agreement ranking one creditor's claim behind another's for payment and enforcement.

hostile.q: If we let you take interest on the shareholder loan, how do we know it won't drain the building when things go wrong?
hostile.a: Because the interest only moves when your distribution test is met, which is the same gate a dividend would pass through. Below a lower coverage level, everything locks up and sweeps to you. I'll give you quarterly reporting and a cure right that requires me to put cash back in before distributions resume. You lose no protection; I just get a cheaper door when the building is healthy.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 58 Review: Doors Home, Withholding and Leakage
summary: Six questions test the week: the four doors, why interest can be cheaper than a dividend, who is liable for wrong withholding, the three gates before a distribution, the leakage stack, and gross-up arithmetic. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical distribution memo, and a boardroom drill asks you to explain repatriation in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: profit abroad comes home through one of four doors, each with its own tax and legal gate, so build the doors early, use them on schedule, and measure everything lost on the way.

Recall

Q. What are the six layers of the leakage stack?

A. Project-country corporate tax, withholding, home tax after credit or exemption, currency conversion cost, compliance cost, and the time cost of money waiting to move.

Q. Why should substance be built before the first payment rather than later?

A. Because the record of who decided, and where, must exist at the time of each decision; it cannot be created afterward for payments already made.

Q. Why do owners review the contractor's baseline schedule before accepting it?

A. Because once accepted, it becomes the measure for progress, delay and claims; errors in logic or float ownership accepted at the start are fought over later.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every investor you bring in will judge you on the cash they receive, not the profit you report. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can design and defend a repatriation plan. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the four doors and the legal basis each needs.

Answer: A dividend needs distributable profit or a passed solvency test. Interest needs a real, documented loan on commercial terms. A fee needs a real service at an arm's-length price. A return of capital needs recorded paid-up capital and the formal corporate steps for a reduction.

Question 2. Why can interest deliver more cash home than a dividend from the same profit?

Answer: Interest is usually deductible to the project, so it avoids project-country corporate tax, and it is then taxed once, at withholding and home tax. A dividend is paid from profit already taxed, then withheld on. Interest caps and thin-capitalisation rules limit how far this can go.

Question 3. If a reduced treaty rate is wrongly applied to a dividend, who usually pays the shortfall?

Answer: The payer, as collection agent, which is usually your own project company, plus interest and possibly penalties, after the money has left.

Question 4. Name the three gates every distribution must pass.

Answer: The corporate-law test, the loan's distribution conditions, and the withholding obligation with its supporting evidence.

Question 5. What is trapped cash, and how should you value it?

Answer: Cash that cannot currently be distributed because of a covenant, missing profit, a capital control or an unbuilt door. Value it below face, discounting for the delay and for currency and banking risk.

Question 6. To deliver 900,000 dollars after 10 percent withholding, what gross dividend is needed?

Answer: 900,000 divided by 0.90, which is 1,000,000 dollars. Gross-ups divide by the share kept.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Devika set out the four doors. Ford and Roman took Argentina in 2001 and 2002, when the doors closed together, giving Rule 58. Nadia built the leakage stack and priced trapped cash. Elias taught withholding as the payer's duty, and the corporate and loan gates. Devika reverse engineered a cash target through every door, including indirect tax on fees. Roman negotiated distribution terms with a lender.

The Red Pen

Find the defects in this hypothetical distribution memo before reading on.

Distribution Memo, Q3. Propco will pay 1,200,000 dollars to Holdco: 800,000 dollars as a dividend and 400,000 dollars as a development management fee for the quarter. Withholding: treaty rate of 5 percent applied to both, per Holdco's request. Trailing DSCR is 1.28 against a 1.30 distribution test; the fee is outside the test as an operating cost. Distributable profit: not yet calculated; the accounts will be finalised after year end. Cash remaining after payment: 50,000 dollars against payables of 300,000 dollars due next month. Approved by the asset manager.

The defects. First, the DSCR of 1.28 fails the 1.30 test, so the dividend is blocked. Second, labelling 400,000 dollars as a fee to get around the test, with no described service, is a disguised distribution and likely a default. Third, the 5 percent rate is applied to the fee as if a dividend rate covered it; fees have their own withholding, possibly no treaty reduction, and possibly indirect tax. Fourth, the treaty rate is applied on Holdco's request, with no residence certificate or beneficial-ownership evidence on file. Fifth, distributable profit has not been calculated, so the corporate test cannot be shown to pass. Sixth, 50,000 dollars of cash against 300,000 dollars of payables suggests the company would fail a solvency test after paying. Seventh, an asset manager is not the board; the dividend needs a resolution by those with authority.

Now write the corrected memo in three lines: no dividend this quarter, because the DSCR test fails and solvency is not shown; no fee unless a defined service was performed and priced, with its own withholding and indirect tax; and a board paper next quarter, with distributable profit, solvency, covenant and withholding each evidenced. Most defects in a distribution memo are payments that should not be made at all.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "How do we actually get paid from the foreign project?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Profit abroad comes home through four doors: dividends, interest on our shareholder loan, fees for real services, and return of the capital we put in. Each is taxed differently. Interest is deductible to the project, so it usually leaks less than a dividend, within limits on how much debt the project can carry. Fees must be for real work, and can carry indirect tax. Return of capital mostly defers tax to the sale. Every payment must pass three gates: corporate law, the lender's distribution test, and withholding at the right rate with the evidence to support it, because the project company pays if we get it wrong. We measure leakage every year, everything lost between project profit and cash in your hands, and we sweep cash home on a fixed schedule so it is never trapped if a country changes its rules. That is the lesson of Argentina."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the four doors and the three gates? Did you mention leakage and the sweep? Did you finish inside two minutes?

Then record it a second time, tomorrow, and listen for one thing: did you use the word "door" for each of the four channels and the word "gate" for each of the three tests? Fixed words for fixed ideas make an explanation easier to follow by ear, and an investor who hears the same word twice remembers it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a distribution that passes one gate and fails another. The control: a distribution memo that checks corporate law, covenants and withholding, in that order, with evidence, every time.

One more test before you close the week. Take any one of your own past cross-border payments, or a hypothetical one if you have none, and name its door, its three gates and its leakage layers aloud in under a minute. If any part is vague, that is the part to review first next week.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking the cheapest door on a spreadsheet is the right one. The right door is the cheapest one that passes all three gates and survives an audit.

Callback

In Week 38, JAX and Elias taught waterfalls and the tax character of developer fees. Repatriation is the cross-border cousin of the waterfall: the same cash, divided by priority, with every slice carrying its own tax label.

Recap

Four doors, three gates, one leakage stack, and a sweep schedule. Rule 58 keeps distributable cash moving through tested doors rather than waiting behind closed ones.

head: The six questions
speak: Repatriation this week came down to four doors, three gates and one stack. The doors are dividends from distributable profit, interest on a documented loan, fees for real services at arm's length, and return of recorded capital. Interest usually leaks less than a dividend because it is deductible, within debt limits; fees can carry indirect tax; return of capital defers tax to the sale. Every payment must pass three gates: the corporate-law test, the lender's distribution conditions, and withholding at the right rate with evidence, because the project company pays if it is wrong. I measure leakage each year in six layers, from corporate tax to the time money waits, and I value trapped cash below its face. Argentina in 2001 and 2002 showed that doors can close together, fast. Rule 58: never let distributable cash accumulate behind a door I have not tested; move it on a fixed schedule.
terms: Disguised distribution — a payment labelled as a fee, loan or expense that is in substance a distribution of profit to the owner.
Paid-up capital — the amount shareholders have actually contributed to a company, recorded as capital in its accounts and corporate records.
Distribution memo — a written check, before any payment to owners, that the corporate test, the loan conditions and the withholding obligation are each met.

hostile.q: Your plan pays us partly as fees. Why isn't that just a dividend in disguise?
hostile.a: Because each fee is for a defined service our company actually performs, under a written agreement, at a price supported by a pricing analysis, and it carries its own withholding and indirect tax. If a service is not performed, the fee is not paid. Where the cash is really a return on capital, we pay it as a dividend or return of capital, through the lender's distribution test, and we accept the tax that comes with it.
